questionText: In a pictograph, 🍎 = 5 apples. If Monday shows 🍎🍎🍎, how many apples were sold?
questionLatex: In a pictograph, 🍎 = 5 apples. If Monday shows 🍎🍎🍎, how many apples were sold?
hints: This is a pictograph question. Each picture stands for more than one thing, so look at the key first.
Count how many apple pictures Monday shows. Each one stands for 5 apples.
A similar example: one star picture stands for 4 books and Tuesday shows 6 stars. 6 × 4 = 24 books.

stepByStep.text: The key says each picture stands for 5 apples.

misconceptions.A: This is 3 + 5. Each of the 3 pictures stands for 5 apples, so multiply instead of adding.
misconceptions.B: Yes! 3 pictures of 5 apples each make 3 × 5 = 15 apples.
misconceptions.C: 5 is what one picture stands for. Monday shows 3 pictures.
misconceptions.D: 3 is the number of pictures. Each picture stands for 5 apples, so multiply by 5.

questionText: In a bar graph, the tallest bar represents:
questionLatex: In a bar graph, the tallest bar represents:
hints: This question is about reading a bar graph. Think about what the height of a bar tells you.
Imagine a bar graph of marks. A child with more marks gets a taller bar. So what does the tallest bar show?
A similar example: in a bar graph of rainfall, the shortest bar belongs to the month with the least rain. The height of a bar always matches the size of its value.

stepByStep.text: In a bar graph, the height of each bar shows how big its value is.
A bigger value gets a taller bar.
So the tallest bar represents the largest value.

misconceptions.A: The average is found by adding all the values and sharing equally. It is not shown by the tallest bar. Think about what a taller bar means.
misconceptions.B: A value of zero would have no bar at all. A tall bar means a big value.
misconceptions.C: Yes! The taller the bar, the larger the value.
misconceptions.D: The smallest value has the shortest bar. Think about what the tallest one means.

questionText: The mean of 12, 15, 18, 21, 24 is:
hints: This asks for the mean, which is another word for average. It is the fair share if the total were split equally.
First add all five numbers together. Then think about how many numbers there are.
A similar example: the mean of 4, 6, 8, 10 and 12. Add them: 4 + 6 + 8 + 10 + 12 = 40. There are 5 numbers, so 40 ÷ 5 = 8. The mean is 8.

stepByStep.text: There are 5 numbers, so divide the total by 5.

misconceptions.A: Yes! The total is 90 and 90 ÷ 5 = 18.
misconceptions.B: 15 is one of the numbers, but not the fair share. Add all five numbers and divide by 5.
misconceptions.C: Check your total. The five numbers add up to 90, and then you divide by 5.
misconceptions.D: 90 is the total of the numbers. To get the mean, divide the total by how many numbers there are.

questionText: The mode of 3, 5, 7, 5, 9, 5, 2 is:
hints: This asks for the mode. The mode is the number that appears most often in a list.
Go through the list and count how many times each number appears. A tally can help.
A similar example: in 4, 8, 6, 8, 1, 8, 6 the number 8 appears three times and 6 appears twice. Nothing appears more often than 8, so the mode is 8.

stepByStep.text: Count how many times each number appears in 3, 5, 7, 5, 9, 5, 2.
5 appears 3 times. Every other number appears only once.

misconceptions.A: Yes! 5 appears three times, more than any other number.
misconceptions.B: 9 is the biggest number, but the mode is the one that appears most often. Count each number.
misconceptions.C: 7 appears only once. Look for the number that shows up the most times.
misconceptions.D: 3 is the first number in the list, but it appears only once. Look for the number that shows up the most.

questionText: The range of 14, 8, 22, 5, 17 is:
hints: This asks for the range. The range tells you how far apart the biggest and smallest numbers are.
Find the biggest number and the smallest number in the list. You will need both.
A similar example: the range of 6, 19, 11, 3 and 15. The biggest is 19 and the smallest is 3. 19 − 3 = 16, so the range is 16.

stepByStep.text: The biggest number is 22 and the smallest is 5.
Subtract the smallest from the biggest.

misconceptions.A: This is 22 + 5. For the range, subtract the smallest from the biggest instead of adding.
misconceptions.B: 14 is the first number in the list. The range is the biggest number minus the smallest.
misconceptions.C: 5 is the smallest number. The range is how far it is from the biggest number.
misconceptions.D: Yes! 22 − 5 = 17, so the range is 17.

questionText: In a pictograph, ☺ = 10 students. ☺☺½ represents:
hints: This is a pictograph question with a half picture. A half picture stands for half of what a full one stands for.
Count the full pictures first and work out what they stand for. Then find what half a picture is worth.
A similar example: one picture stands for 8 toys, and a row shows 3 full pictures and a half. 3 × 8 = 24, and half of 8 is 4. 24 + 4 = 28 toys.

stepByStep.text: Each full picture stands for 10 students. There are 2 full pictures.
The half picture stands for half of 10.

misconceptions.A: Yes! Two full pictures make 20 and the half makes 5 more, so 25.
misconceptions.B: This counts one full picture and a half. There are two full pictures before the half.
misconceptions.C: This counts only the two full pictures. The half picture stands for 5 more students.
misconceptions.D: This counts the half picture as a full one. Half a picture stands for 5 students, not 10.

questionText: Bar A = 45, Bar B = 30. Difference:
hints: This asks for the difference between two bars. Difference means how much more one is than the other.
To find a difference, take the smaller value away from the bigger one.
A similar example: one bar shows 62 and another shows 40. 62 − 40 = 22, so the difference is 22.

stepByStep.text: Difference means subtract the smaller value from the bigger one.
Bar A is 45 and Bar B is 30.

misconceptions.A: Check your subtraction. 45 − 30 leaves 1 ten and 5 ones.
misconceptions.B: This is 45 + 30. Difference means subtract, not add.
misconceptions.C: This is 45 ÷ 30. Difference means subtract the smaller from the bigger.

questionText: If you toss a coin, getting a head is:
questionLatex: If you toss a coin, getting a head is:
hints: This is about chance. Think about all the things that can happen when you toss a coin.
A coin has two sides, heads and tails. Is one side more likely to land face up than the other?
A similar example: a bag has 5 red balls and 5 blue balls. Each colour has the same number of balls, so picking red has the same chance as picking blue.

stepByStep.text: A coin has two sides: heads and tails.
Both sides have the same chance of landing face up.
So getting a head is equally likely as tails.

misconceptions.A: Certain means it must happen every time. A coin can also land on tails. Compare the chances of the two sides.
misconceptions.B: Yes! Heads and tails each have the same chance.
misconceptions.C: Impossible means it can never happen. A coin does land on heads sometimes. Compare the chances of the two sides.
misconceptions.D: Likely means it happens more often than not. Heads does not come up more often than tails. The two sides have the same chance.

questionText: A table shows: Mon=12, Tue=15, Wed=18, Thu=10, Fri=20. Total:
questionLatex: A table shows: Mon=12, Tue=15, Wed=18, Thu=10, Fri=20. Total:
hints: This asks for a total from a table. Total means add all the values together.
Add the numbers a few at a time. Look for pairs that make easy tens, like 12 and 18.
A similar example: Mon = 11, Tue = 14, Wed = 9, Thu = 16. Pair them up: 11 + 9 = 20 and 14 + 16 = 30. Then 20 + 30 = 50 in total.

misconceptions.A: This is 10 too few. Check that all five days are added in.
misconceptions.C: This is 5 too many. Add again slowly, pairing 12 with 18 and 10 with 20.
misconceptions.D: This is 5 too few. Check the ones digits when you add the 15.

questionText: Average of 5 numbers is 20. Four numbers are 15, 22, 18, 25. Find the 5th.
questionLatex: Average of 5 numbers is 20. Four numbers are 15, 22, 18, 25. Find the 5th.
hints: This is an average problem worked backwards. If you know the average and how many numbers there are, you can find their total.
First find the total of all five numbers. Multiply the average by how many numbers there are.
A similar example: the average of 4 numbers is 10, and three of them are 8, 12 and 9. The total must be 4 × 10 = 40. The three known numbers add up to 29. 40 − 29 = 11, so the fourth number is 11.

stepByStep.text: The total of all 5 numbers is the average times 5.
Add the four numbers you know.
The fifth number is what is left.

misconceptions.A: Yes! The total must be 100, the four known numbers make 80, and 100 − 80 = 20.
misconceptions.B: 25 is one of the four numbers already given. Find the total of all five, then take away the four you know.
misconceptions.C: 80 is the sum of the four known numbers. Take it away from the total of all five.
misconceptions.D: 100 is the total of all five numbers. Take away the four you know to find the fifth.

questionText: An event that will definitely happen is called:
questionLatex: An event that will definitely happen is called:
hints: This is about the words we use for chance. Each word tells how sure we are that something will happen.
Think of something that must happen, like the sun rising tomorrow. Which word says there is no doubt at all?
A similar example: picking a green ball from a bag that has only red balls can never happen. An event that can never happen is called impossible.

stepByStep.text: Some events may or may not happen. Others can never happen.
An event that will definitely happen has no doubt about it.
Such an event is called certain.

misconceptions.A: Uncertain means we are not sure. The question says the event will definitely happen.
misconceptions.B: Impossible means it can never happen. That is the opposite of what the question asks.
misconceptions.C: Yes! Certain means it will definitely happen.
misconceptions.D: Unlikely means it probably will not happen. Look for the word that means it will surely happen.

questionText: In a pie chart, if 'Cricket' takes up 1/4 of the circle, the angle is:
questionLatex: In a pie chart, if 'Cricket' takes up 1/4 of the circle, the angle is:
hints: This is about a pie chart. A full circle has 360 degrees at its centre, and each slice takes a share of that.
The slice is one quarter of the circle. So you need one quarter of the full turn of 360 degrees.
A similar example: a slice that takes up 1/6 of the circle. 360 ÷ 6 = 60, so its angle is 60 degrees.

misconceptions.A: 45° is one eighth of the circle. One quarter is 360 ÷ 4.
misconceptions.B: 180° is half of the circle. One quarter is smaller than that.
misconceptions.C: 120° is one third of the circle. For one quarter, divide 360 by 4.
misconceptions.D: Yes! One quarter of 360° is 90°.

questionText: Find the median of: 7, 3, 9, 5, 11.
hints: This asks for the median. The median is the middle number once the list is in order.
First write the numbers from smallest to biggest. Do not pick the middle one until they are in order.
A similar example: the median of 8, 2, 6, 12 and 4. In order they are 2, 4, 6, 8, 12. The middle one is 6, so the median is 6.

stepByStep.text: There are 5 numbers, so the middle one is the third.

misconceptions.A: 3 is the smallest number. The median is the middle number after putting them in order.
misconceptions.B: 5 is the second number in order. Count to the middle of the five numbers.
misconceptions.C: 9 is in the middle of the list as it is written. Put the numbers in order first, then find the middle.
misconceptions.D: Yes! In order the numbers are 3, 5, 7, 9, 11 and 7 is in the middle.

questionText: 36 books need to be shown. If each symbol = 6 books, how many symbols?
questionLatex: 36 books need to be shown. If each symbol = 6 books, how many symbols?
hints: This is a pictograph question worked backwards. You know the total and what one symbol stands for, and you need the number of symbols.
Think of putting the 36 books into equal groups. Each group is one symbol.
A similar example: 56 pencils are shown and each symbol stands for 8 pencils. 56 ÷ 8 = 7, so 7 symbols are needed.

stepByStep.text: Each symbol stands for 6 books. Share 36 books into groups of 6.

misconceptions.A: This is 36 − 6. You need to find how many groups of 6 fit into 36, so divide.
misconceptions.B: This is 36 × 6. The symbols group the books, so divide instead of multiplying.
misconceptions.C: 5 symbols show only 5 × 6 = 30 books. You need enough symbols for all 36.
misconceptions.D: Yes! 36 ÷ 6 = 6 symbols.

questionText: A bar graph has scale: 1 cm = 20 students. A bar is 3.5 cm tall. Students:
questionLatex: A bar graph has scale: 1 cm = 20 students. A bar is 3.5 cm tall. Students:
hints: This is about the scale of a bar graph. The scale tells you how many students each centimetre of bar stands for.
Split the height of the bar into 3 whole centimetres and half a centimetre. Work out what each part stands for.
A similar example: the scale is 1 cm = 10 students and a bar is 4.5 cm tall. 4 cm stands for 4 × 10 = 40 students, and half a centimetre stands for 5. 40 + 5 = 45 students.

stepByStep.text: Each centimetre stands for 20 students. Start with the 3 whole centimetres.
Half a centimetre stands for half of 20.

misconceptions.A: 3.5 is the height of the bar in centimetres. Each centimetre stands for 20 students, so multiply.
misconceptions.B: Yes! 3.5 × 20 = 70 students.
misconceptions.C: This is 3.5 × 10. The scale says each centimetre stands for 20 students.
misconceptions.D: This counts only the 3 whole centimetres. The extra half centimetre stands for 10 more students.

questionText: Rolling a 7 on a standard die (1-6) is:
questionLatex: Rolling a 7 on a standard die (1-6) is:
hints: This is about chance. Think about which numbers a die can show.
List the numbers on the faces of a standard die. Is 7 one of them?
A similar example: rolling a number less than 7 on a standard die. Every face shows a number from 1 to 6, so this happens on every roll. That event is certain.

stepByStep.text: A standard die has six faces showing 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 and 6.
There is no face with 7 on it, so a 7 can never come up.

misconceptions.A: Yes! A die has no 7, so a 7 can never be rolled.
misconceptions.B: Certain means it happens every time. Check which numbers are on a die.
misconceptions.C: Unlikely means it can happen, but not often. Check whether a die has a 7 at all.
misconceptions.D: Likely means it happens often. Check whether a die has a 7 at all.

stepByStep.text: Go through the list and tick each 8: 8, 9, 8, 10, 9, 8, 7, 9, 8, 10.

misconceptions.B: Yes! The mark 8 appears 4 times.

questionText: Average of 4 numbers is 25. Three numbers are 20, 30, 22. Find the fourth.
questionLatex: Average of 4 numbers is 25. Three numbers are 20, 30, 22. Find the fourth.
hints: This is an average problem worked backwards. The average and the count of numbers together tell you the total.
First find the total of all four numbers. Multiply the average by how many numbers there are.
A similar example: the average of 3 numbers is 12, and two of them are 9 and 13. The total must be 3 × 12 = 36. The two known numbers add up to 22. 36 − 22 = 14, so the third number is 14.

stepByStep.text: The total of all 4 numbers is the average times 4.
Add the three numbers you know.
The fourth number is what is left.

misconceptions.A: 25 is the average, not the missing number. Find the total of all four, then take away the three you know.
misconceptions.B: Check your adding. 20 + 30 + 22 = 72, and that comes off the total of 100.
misconceptions.C: Yes! The total must be 100, the three known numbers make 72, and 100 − 72 = 28.
misconceptions.D: Check the total first. Four numbers with an average of 25 add up to 4 × 25 = 100. Then take away 72.
